title: Your own commentary
hook: writing notes in the margin of your life
tomorrow: Eli asks a question Noa can't answer. does she have to answer it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Preida and the lesson said four hundred times more. Teach it: the teaching finishes the learning. Today, the learning talks back.

A used paperback from a thrift store, and someone has written in it. An underline. A question mark. A furious no! beside a plot twist. Sometimes the notes are the best part. So who writes in a holy book? In Jewish tradition, readers do, starting with the very first verse. Rashi, the medieval commentator, stops at the Torah's opening words, In the beginning, and says something odd about them. This verse, he writes, says only one thing: interpret me.
screen: `A FURIOUS NO! IN THE MARGIN.` → `WHO WRITES IN A HOLY BOOK?` → `THIS VERSE SAYS: INTERPRET ME.`

segments.voice: Why would the first verse need help? Rashi explains himself. If the verse meant to teach the order of creation, he says, it would have been worded differently. The way it's written doesn't settle what came first. So he doesn't pretend it does. He leaves a note: this one is asking you to dig. Here's the puzzle solved. The Torah, in this way of reading, isn't a finished statement you file away. It's one side of a conversation, and the reader is expected to answer. That's why a printed page of the Talmud looks the way it does: the old text in the middle, and later voices in the margins around it, Rashi's notes running down the inside edge. Nobody erased the text to make room. They wrote next to it. Your own commentary works the same way. A verse about seeking a city's peace, and in the margin, the name of your street. A line about honoring parents, and beside it, a question you still can't answer about your own. You aren't changing the verse. You're showing where it touched you. Something to tell a friend tonight: one of Judaism's great commentators read the Torah's first sentence and wrote, in effect, this one needs a reader.
screen: `WHY DOES THE FIRST VERSE NEED HELP?` · `ONE SIDE OF A CONVERSATION.` · `THE TEXT IN THE MIDDLE, VOICES AROUND.` · `SHOWING WHERE IT TOUCHED YOU.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN MARGIN.`

segments.voice: Pick one verse or line you know, from these lessons or from memory, and write it by hand. Underneath, in small letters, write one comment: a question it raises, a person it reminds you of, or a place in your week where it fits. Read the two together once, slowly.
screen: `ONE VERSE, BY HAND.` · `ONE COMMENT UNDERNEATH.` · `READ THEM TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Your own commentary: notes in the margin of a text, and of a life. The verse stays the same; your answer to it is yours.
Pocket this one: your own margin, because even the first verse of the Torah asked for a reader. Talk soon.

howItsDone: Jewish learners often read the Torah and Talmud alongside commentaries such as Rashi's, and some keep their own notes in the margins of a personal Chumash or study book.

chat.says: found saba's old chumash for eli. it's FULL of pencil notes. is that even allowed in a holy book??
options: Allowed. Rashi wrote that the first verse says interpret me. Notes are your answer.
Not really. Holy books stay clean; notes belong in a separate notebook.
Only a rabbi's notes count. Saba's are just doodles in the margin.
chat.meaning: Jewish tradition reads with a pen: the text in the middle, voices around it. Saba's notes are his commentary, his side of the conversation.

Rashi.meaning: a medieval commentator whose notes run beside the Torah and Talmud

Torah.meaning: the Five Books of Moses; also, Jewish teaching as a whole

Talmud.meaning: the great collection of rabbinic discussion built on the Mishnah

commentary.meaning: notes that explain or question a text, written beside it

sources.ref: Rashi on Genesis 1:1 (this verse says only: interpret me; it does not come to teach the order of creation)
